chapter_title: A Catechumen asked the Apostle: When I would give

fills.notes: The sequence is: strike → make sore/wound → strike again and do further harm. The next clause speaks of blows over blows; a verb of additional injury fits the forensic comparison.
Corresponds to the following phrase 'and he hits over his blows': the idiom is iterative violence (adding strokes), preparing for the judge inspecting accumulated marks.
Introduces the set of blows already mentioned: 'the blows that have made sores'.
Subject resumes: the opponent 'strikes him these two times'.
Connects the double striking to the subsequent legal action (going to the judge).
The judge questions about the measurable evidence: the count/measure of sores left as marks. Fits correspondentially: judgment in ultimates is by 'marks' and 'measure'.
Copula in 'as he is judged ... according to enmity'.
The condemned enemy is judged for retaliation, specifically for retaliating though no prior sin was against him (stated at end of ¶4).
Transitions from legal punishment to the other case: sickness leading to medical treatment.
The wound 'comes out' as a manifestation; correspondentially illness emerges from an interior cause, contrasting with externally inflicted wounds.
He becomes sick by illness and '...'—a verb of undergoing/bearing fits before calling the doctor.
Doctor has no '...' nor '...': standard pairing is remedy/means (drug) and incantation or charm. In the oldest technical register: practical means.
Contrasts with knife/surgery: no charm/spell, but incision. Keeps pre-institutional, non-devotional tone while reflecting common ancient medical pairings.
After healing, the patient rewards the physician: 'He shall even make ... gifts and compliments'—the indirect object is the doctor.
The whole exemplum is about distinguishing retaliation (evil) from corrective cutting (healing). This line applies it to the soul: 'matter of healing before this living soul'.
Introduces the application/explanation after the analogies.
Matches the medical figure: the soul is 'cut' (disciplined/purged) at a certain time; prepares for 'it is painful' later.
Needed to negate the appearance of hostile striking: the corrective blow is not enemy-violence.
Object of 'you have struck ...' referring back to the living soul.
Sequence: pain first, then well-being/ease. Fits 'it is well and ... ease shall exist'.
Intensifies 'ease shall exist for it' and aligns with the later 'glory' and 'honour' motif from the doctor analogy.
Directly parallels ¶6: glory comes about for the physician/healer; in application, the agent of corrective healing receives honour.
Glory comes about 'for this doctor/healing'—source/occasion marker.
Bridges 'healing' to its object: healing of the wound/illness of the soul.
Resolves the final contrast: 'it exists ... it is painful ...'—pain precedes the beneficial state, like incision before cure.
Sets the opposite case: not the healer but the hostile striker, matching ¶4-5.
The comrade of the 'living soul' (its companion/kin) is what is struck in the retaliatory/hostile mode; keeps to the chapter’s key term.
He struck the sick with his '...'—correspondentially the opposite of healing is cruelty/violence, matching 'he being cruel'.
He struck 'in ...'—the motive-force in ¶4 is enmity; the judge sentence is 'according to enmity'.
He is cruel according to something; in the oldest register this is wrath/heat of the lower powers, opposed to ordered correction.
Violent striking upon the soul produces guilt/accusation; the text ends with 'accusation of ...'.
Accusation is grounded in the marks/wounds, paralleling ¶4 where the judge inspects the marks as evidence.
Closes the antithesis: accusation belongs to enmity (retaliation), not to healing (benefit).

assessment: Most gaps can be constrained by the chapter’s tight forensic/medical antithesis: hostile retaliation (enmity, accusation, punishment) versus corrective cutting (pain → healing → honour). Exact particles and some nouns (e.g., ‘charm’, ‘wrath’) remain uncertain because the surviving Coptic idiom is not visible; these are restored by correspondential parallelism rather than philology.
